---
title: "What qdaR does"
---


qdaR reads the files the zotQDA and qdaZ Zotero plugins export and computes
the analyses a qualitative study reports. It is a library: there is no
interface, and it does no coding of its own.

This page lists what is in it. For how it stands against MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti and
the rest, see [Comparison](comparison.qmd) — including where those are ahead.

## Reading and validating

| | |
|---|---|
| All nine exchange formats | fragments, uncoded, codebook, history, abbreviations, the three consensus files, multi-coded segments |
| Contract validation | every file declares its kind and version in its first column; a file from a newer format version is refused rather than guessed at |
| Column check | every column the contract promises must be present (`strict=True`); extra columns are always accepted |
| Delimiter and encoding | UTF-8 with BOM, `,` or `;`, detected per file |
| Code identity | `codeId` survives renaming, moving and merging, so an analysis can follow a code across codebook revisions |

## Reading a REFI-QDA project

A `.qdpx` from MAXQDA, ATLAS.ti, NVivo, QDA Miner or Dedoose can be read
directly, which makes this package usable without zotQDA. It supports a
**subset** of the analyses below; `qda_read_qdpx()` names what your particular
file rules out, and [Reading a .qdpx](guide/qdpx.qmd) has the full comparison.

## Agreement between coders

Six coefficients, each with a **95 % percentile bootstrap interval** from a
seeded generator, so the same data gives the same interval here, in qdaR and in
the plugin:

- percentage agreement
- Cohen's kappa — [10.1177/001316446002000104](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316446002000104)
- Brennan and Prediger's kappa — [10.1177/001316448104100307](https://doi.org/10.1177/001316448104100307)
- Fleiss' kappa — [10.1037/h0031619](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0031619)
- Krippendorff's alpha — [10.1080/19312450709336664](https://doi.org/10.1080/19312450709336664)
- Gwet's AC1 — [10.1348/000711006X126600](https://doi.org/10.1348/000711006x126600)

Plus the diagnostics that explain a disappointing coefficient rather than
leaving you with it: prevalence and bias index and PABAK after Feinstein and
Cicchetti ([10.1016/0895-4356(90)90158-L](https://doi.org/10.1016/0895-4356(90)90158-l)),
prevalence with a Wilson interval
([10.1080/01621459.1927.10502953](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1927.10502953)),
agreement per code, and agreement recomputed at each level of the code
hierarchy.

## Did the coders mark the same stretches?

Every coefficient above assumes the segments already correspond. These ask the
prior question:

- **Krippendorff's unitizing alpha** — [10.2307/271061](https://doi.org/10.2307/271061)
- **WindowDiff** and **Pk** — [10.1162/089120102317341756](https://doi.org/10.1162/089120102317341756), [10.1023/A:1007506220214](https://doi.org/10.1023/a:1007506220214)
- **Gamma** after Mathet, Widlöcher and Métivier — [10.1162/COLI_a_00227](https://doi.org/10.1162/coli_a_00227), solved exactly by branch and bound, refusing rather than approximating when the search budget runs out

Text sources only: a PDF rectangle offers no continuum on which boundaries can
be measured.

## Statistics the plugins leave out

- chi-squared with Cramér's V, exact where the expected counts allow it and a
  seeded Monte Carlo test otherwise
- Jaccard code distances
- classical (Torgerson) scaling via `cmdscale`
- hierarchical clustering via `hclust`, with the cophenetic correlation
- correspondence analysis via `MASS::corresp`, reporting the share of
  inertia the map shows

## Planning a study, before there is data

- **Sample size for a kappa confidence interval** — Donner and Rotondi,
  [10.2202/1557-4679.1275](https://doi.org/10.2202/1557-4679.1275); Table 2 of
  that paper is reproduced in all forty-eight cells
- **How many interviews for a theme of a given prevalence** — Fugard and Potts,
  [10.1080/13645579.2015.1005453](https://doi.org/10.1080/13645579.2015.1005453),
  Table 1 reproduced cell for cell

::: {.callout-warning title="Both are contested, and the package says so"}

Braun and Clarke reject sample-size calculation for reflexive thematic
analysis on the ground that themes are constructed rather than counted
([10.1080/13645579.2016.1195588](https://doi.org/10.1080/13645579.2016.1195588)).
That objection belongs next to any number these functions produce.
:::

## Progress and saturation

- new codes per document, in first-coding order
- **saturation as a reportable figure** after Guest, Namey and Chen —
  [10.1371/journal.pone.0232076](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0232076),
  reported as "6+2" with the base, run length and threshold
- the accumulation models of Lowe and colleagues —
  [10.1177/1525822X17749386](https://doi.org/10.1177/1525822x17749386)
- coder drift: the total variation distance between a coder's code
  distribution in successive windows

The saturation figure is **code saturation only**. Hennink, Kaiser and Marconi
([10.1177/1049732316665344](https://doi.org/10.1177/1049732316665344)) show
that meaning saturation arrives considerably later, and Braun and Clarke
([10.1080/2159676X.2019.1704846](https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676x.2019.1704846))
reject the concept for reflexive thematic analysis. The package prints that
caveat with the number.

## Reporting checklists

**COREQ** (32 items, [10.1093/intqhc/mzm042](https://doi.org/10.1093/intqhc/mzm042))
and **SRQR** (21 standards, [10.1097/ACM.0000000000000388](https://doi.org/10.1097/acm.0000000000000388)),
reproduced verbatim and pre-filled where the export knows the answer —
document count, coders, saturation, code system depth. A paraphrased checklist
is one a reviewer cannot match against the original.

COREQ has **no item for intercoder agreement**; SRQR has a home for it in
standard S15. The generated checklists say so.

## Figures

Figures are drawn with **ggplot2**, and every `qda_plot_*` function returns
an ordinary ggplot object: add a theme, change a scale, put it in a patchwork.

The plugin's own Vega-Lite specifications render unchanged through
`qda_spec_render()` (vegawidget), for the case where a figure has to match
what Zotero showed.

Every plot has a table behind it, exposed separately — `qda_code_counts()`,
`qda_code_matrix()`, `qda_timeline()`, `qda_saturation()`: the numbers behind
a figure are what goes into a paper.

## What it deliberately does not do

- **No coding.** That is zotQDA's job, in Zotero's reader.
- **No interface.** Non-programmers want qdaZ.
- **No writing.** qdaR never modifies your Zotero library; it reads files.
- **No text mining beyond counting.** Word frequencies and keyword in context
  live in qdaZ; stemming, lemmatisation and topic models are not here, and a
  half-implemented version would be worse than none.
- **No AI.**

## How the numbers are checked

Every coefficient is computed twice: once by the plugin in JavaScript, once
here. Frozen reference files hold randomly generated coder matrices together
with the plugin's results, and the test suite compares to twelve decimal
places. The same files are byte-identical in qdaPy, and a test asserts that, so
three implementations in three languages are held against one reference rather
than against each other.

Where a published worked example exists, it is reproduced rather than
paraphrased: Krippendorff's unitizing example, Donner and Rotondi's Table 2 in
all forty-eight cells, Fugard and Potts' Table 1, Mathet's Figure 11.

Agreement between three implementations shows they are consistent. Agreement
with a published table shows they are right.
